title: EPIC study of Michigan school district responses to the COVID-19 pandemic
description: The Education Policy Innovation Collaborative (EPIC) at Michigan State University is conducting a study of "Michigan school district responses to the COVID-19 pandemic and efforts to support student learning." article_title: AI Advice Suppresses People's Willingness to Say \"I Don't Know\", Even When the Advice Is Wrong and Accuracy Is Incentivized
citation: Chiara Marcoccia, Walter Quattrociocchi, Valerio Capraro. (2026). AI advice suppresses people's willingness to say "I don't know", even when the advice is wrong and accuracy is incentivized. https://osf.io/nwx6r/overview?view_only=a03ae0ca587c4c84a442c44d55ab97b6
title: Epistemia: acceptance of AI output for surface fluency lowers the metacognitive threshold for answering
description: The article reads its findings through epistemia, "the tendency to accept AI outputs for their surface plausibility and syntactic coherence rather than through verification". Because an LLM must always produce an output and does not itself suspend judgment, users who delegate judgment to it may inherit that lack of suspension. The authors propose that a fluent available answer lowers the threshold at which people decide they know enough to respond, reducing suspension, inflating confidence, and lowering accuracy when the advice is wrong.
requirements: An AI system that always produces a fluent output, so that an answer is available even when the user lacks knowledge
constraints: The article states it is untested whether suspension collapses to the same degree when AI advice is usually correct
The design did not record whether participants who overrode the AI consulted other sources, limiting inferences about verification
target_learners: Adult online participants answering knowledge questions
Users of AI assistants, search summaries, and writing tools
target_learning_goals: Calibrated judgment about whether one knows enough to answer
Willingness to withhold an answer under uncertainty
examples: The authors propose that the availability of a fluent answer lowers the threshold for responding, with stakes one condition under which this mechanism partly re-engages.

article_title: Amid an Epistemic Iteration: How AI Methodologies May Transform the Nature of Science Education Research
citation: Paul P. Martin, Marvin Rost, Jenna Koenen, Nicole Graulich. (2026). Amid an Epistemic Iteration: How AI Methodologies May Transform the Nature of Science Education Research. Science & Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11191-026-00789-7
title: Epistemic iteration as a lens on AI's transformation of science education research, with a three-stage analogy to measurement of student learning
description: Drawing on Chang (2004), the article defines epistemic iteration as "successive stages of knowledge that build iteratively on one another to achieve specific epistemic aims." It argues AI methodologies may mark a new stage in science education research's own epistemic iteration, paralleling thermometry's stages. The analogy maps a first stage of personal empiricism, a second of relative comparisons as in classical test theory, and a third of formalized measurement models such as item-response theory and Rasch modeling, with AI offering possible further improvement.
requirements: The analogy is used in Chang's practice-based sense of measurement as an evolving system of practice that renders phenomena observable
constraints: The authors acknowledge the analogy "may fall short in certain respects" because analyzing student learning is context-dependent and AI methodologies are data-analysis methods, not measurement instruments themselves
target_learning_goals: understanding methodological change in a research field through history and philosophy of science
examples: The article parallels the replacement of water's boiling point with its steam point to argue AI's usefulness "must be empirically examined" through sustained cycles of testing and comparison
key_sources: Paul P. Martin, Marvin Rost, Jenna Koenen, Nicole Graulich. (2026). Amid an Epistemic Iteration: How AI Methodologies May Transform the Nature of Science Education Research. Science & Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11191-026-00789-7

article_title: Faculty Orientations Shape Adoption of AI in Research and Teaching
citation: T. J. Atherton, I. Descamps, M. Webel, T. R. Holmes, C. L. Vizcarra, N. Sui, J. J. Foley IV. (2026). Faculty Orientations Shape Adoption of AI in Research and Teaching. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.18140
title: Proposed model of AI adoption in which epistemic interpretation of AI shapes the relationship between sentiments and practical use
description: The article proposes a model in which faculty adoption of AI is driven not primarily by access, social influence, or perceived utility, but by how instructors interpret AI's role in disciplinary thinking and knowledge production. As the authors state, "We therefore propose a model of AI adoption where epistemic interpretation of AI shapes the relationship between sentiments of AI and its practical use." Faculty differ not in whether they see benefits and risks, but in how they interpret AI's role in disciplinary thinking; those oriented away see AI as potentially undermining careful engagement needed for expertise, while those oriented toward it value delegating ancillary thinking with risks treated as constraints. The construct of AI pedagogical orientation operationalizes this account.
requirements: The model was developed for a targeted population of pedagogically motivated STEM faculty (RCSA Cottrell awardees) surveyed at a particular moment in AI adoption
constraints: The authors note external factors currently not driving adoption may become relevant at later stages as technologies, information, and institutional responses mature
target_learning_goals: Understanding and supporting faculty adoption and integration of AI (LLMs) in research and teaching
examples: The model was built from a mixed-methods survey of 90 Cottrell faculty combining EFA, logistic regression, and qualitative coding of open-ended responses
key_sources: T. J. Atherton, I. Descamps, M. Webel, T. R. Holmes, C. L. Vizcarra, N. Sui, J. J. Foley IV. (2026). Faculty Orientations Shape Adoption of AI in Research and Teaching. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.18140

article_title: The critical-thinking paradox in generative AI-integrated learning: distinguishing efficiency from cognitive depth — a differentiated framework and testable propositions
citation: Lin J and Al-Hada NM (2026) The critical-thinking paradox in generative AI-integrated learning: distinguishing efficiency from cognitive depth—a differentiated framework and testable propositions. Front. Psychol. 17:1906070. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1906070
title: Episodic–habitual offloading distinction and the cognitive-debt construct
description: The article's original extension is "the distinction between episodic offloading—the deliberate, task-specific delegation of an operation while retaining awareness of what is offloaded and why—and habitual offloading—routine, weakly monitored reliance that may recalibrate expected cognitive effort". It adopts "cognitive debt to denote a potential cumulative reduction in metacognitive calibration and/or unaided higher-order cognitive performance that persists beyond a particular AI-assisted episode". A proposed cognitive-debt cycle runs from routine AI use through reduced engagement, weakened calibration practice, and increased reliance, but is explicitly treated as a hypothesis requiring prospective longitudinal tests, not an established sequence.
requirements: For construct validity, cognitive debt must be operationalized as a within-person deterioration from baseline in outcomes measured without AI, after controlling for prior knowledge and practice, separable from offloading frequency and dependency.
constraints: The cognitive-debt cycle is not yet an established longitudinal sequence; the observational paths cited do not establish that routine AI use causes declining engagement.
target_learners: learners and teachers integrating generative AI into study and instruction
target_learning_goals: metacognitive calibration and unaided higher-order cognitive performance
examples: The article hypothesizes three predictors of the transition from episodic to habitual offloading: frequency of unconditioned AI use, low metacognitive monitoring accuracy, and environmental press incentivizing product quality over learning process.

article_title: Evidence of a Cognitive Shift in AI Education: How Students Are Rethinking Human Intelligence?
citation: Islem Rekik. (2026). Evidence of a Cognitive Shift in AI Education: How Students Are Rethinking Human Intelligence? Published as a conference paper at ICLR HCAIR Workshop 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.16292
title: Epistemic self-defense: practices protecting beliefs, knowledge, and reasoning from deception and epistemic harm
description: The article introduces epistemic self-defense as "the set of cognitive, metacognitive, and social practices individuals use to protect their beliefs, knowledge, and reasoning processes from deception, error, manipulation, or epistemic harm." It frames this as the ability to defend one's epistemic agency where information is abundant, persuasive, or unreliable. It offers this as one explanation for the post-2023 shift: students becoming aware that AI outputs can shape human judgement, not merely assist it.
requirements: Environments where information is abundant, persuasive, or unreliable
constraints: The article presents this as one possible explanation for the observed shift, not a tested result
target_learners: Students using generative AI in academic work
target_learning_goals: Protecting epistemic agency
Maintaining standards of evidence and epistemic ownership
examples: The article cites epistemic self-defense as an explanation for students' post-2023 reinvestment in human intelligence.

article_title: Constructing Epistemic AI Literacy: Detecting Epistemic Aims and Processes in Student-AI Co-Programming
citation: Menggian Wu. (2026). Constructing Epistemic AI Literacy: Detecting Epistemic Aims and Processes in Student-AI Co-Programming. 2nd International Workshop on AI Literacy Education For All (ALIT4ALL 2026), co-located with AIED 2026, Seoul, Republic of Korea.
title: Epistemic AI Literacy (EAIL): a process-oriented framework for AI literacy grounded in the AIR framework
description: EAIL reframes AI literacy as a process-oriented epistemic phenomenon enacted during human-GenAI interaction, defined as the ability to understand, regulate, and critically engage with AI as cognitive agents, including deciding when to trust, outsource, verify, justify, and override AI judgments. Drawing on the AIR framework of epistemic aims, ideals, and reliable processes, it operationalizes literacy at the level of prompt-response pairs rather than through trait-like self-report scales. The article argues that 'AI literacy is most clearly enacted during direct interaction with AI systems, especially when learners engage in tasks that require higher order thinking.'
requirements: Analysis requires authentic human-AI interaction data, with the prompt-response pair as the unit of analysis
constraints: The study only focuses on detecting and describing epistemic aims and epistemic processes, not all AIR components simultaneously
target_learners: undergraduate programming students using generative AI
target_learning_goals: critical and epistemically productive engagement with AI-generated knowledge
examples: Applied to 200 sampled co-programming chat sessions from the StudyChat corpus to profile students' epistemic performance

article_title: Pathways to Learning: Exploring High School Students' Learning of AI-Powered Educational Robotics
citation: G. McLaughlin, E. Novak, S. Ahmadi, J. Li, Y. Guo, R. Liu, & L. Borgerding. (2026). Pathways to learning: exploring high school students' learning of AI-powered educational robotics. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10651-w
title: Epistemological pluralism as a framework for robotics and AI learning pathways
description: The study draws on constructionism and Turkle and Papert's epistemological pluralism, which "emphasizes that there are multiple ways of knowing and engaging with the world." Applied to robotics education, the authors argue students build understanding from a spectrum of approaches, from structured rule-based methods to improvisational ones, and that real-world practices, design, and play are legitimate ways of knowing rather than preparatory steps toward real computing.
requirements: A curriculum that intentionally positions aesthetic, narrative, and expressive forms of engagement as legitimate alongside technical programming work
constraints: The authors frame the three themes as situated and exploratory findings from one Midwestern public high school setting, not representative claims
target_learning_goals: robotics concepts
AI and machine learning concepts
computing participation and identity
examples: Students programmed mBots to sort recycling from landfill waste and presented projects at a Celebration of Learning Event, customizing costumes and stories for their robots

article_title: An Educator-Guided LLM Pedagogical Agent for Scaffolded Feedback in Conceptual Database Design
citation: Sara Riazi and Pedram Rooshenas. (2026). An Educator-Guided LLM Pedagogical Agent for Scaffolded Feedback in Conceptual Database Design. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00870v1
title: Episode memory linking feedback episodes to versioned ERD states
description: Each feedback request creates a session history containing stages shown, student answers, generated feedback, follow-up questions, credit use, and next actions, allowing later stages to condition on what has already occurred. "Episodes are linked to saved artifact states through the student, environment, selected relationship, feedback identifier, and ERD version." Returning to the editor ends the episode, and a later request reproceses the current ERD as a new episode rather than assuming the previous diagnosis remains valid. These records support analysis of progression, disclosure, repetition, and subsequent target-level changes, and are not treated as a persistent model of student knowledge.
requirements: Saved artifact states and logged interactions so episodes can be linked to ERD versions and analyzed
constraints: Records coordinate the current episode and are explicitly not a persistent student-knowledge model; a new request after revision creates a new diagnosis
target_learners: Students requesting feedback in an ERD editor
target_learning_goals: Revising conceptual database designs based on staged feedback
examples: The deployment's artifact-interaction-revision traces containing the initiating ERD, hidden context, stages accessed, student responses, and next saved ERD

article_title: From Prompting to Epistemic Proactivity: Temporal Trajectories of Student-AI Interaction in Mathematics Learning
citation: Abdelghani, R., Kaiser, P., Murayama, K. (2026). Changes in Help-Seeking Strategies Predict unaided Performance during AI-based Mathematical Learning. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.28472
title: Epistemic proactivity (EP): the extent to which learners retain responsibility for regulating and advancing their own knowledge-building while using AI
description: Epistemic proactivity characterizes "the extent to which learners retain this responsibility to carry out the important process for learning" during AI-supported learning. It concerns what role learners retain — whether they frame problems and originate learning trajectories or merely react to ones imposed by the AI — and goes beyond prompt sophistication or general engagement by focusing on how responsibility for knowledge-building is distributed between learner and AI. The study operationalizes EP through two behavioral dimensions: SRL functions (plan, monitor, request, evaluate) and the epistemic orientation of help-seeking (understanding-oriented versus closure-oriented requests), and treats EP as a developing property of the interaction rather than a fixed learner characteristic.
requirements: Behavioral codes capture only regulatory functions explicitly expressed in dialogue and should not be interpreted as a complete measure of internal self-regulation.
constraints: EP does not assume learners should perform every cognitive or regulatory operation independently; delegation becomes problematic when the learner increasingly relies on the model for determining what to pursue, generating reasoning, and judging understanding.
target_learning_goals: mathematical modelling with linear and quadratic functions
examples: The study coded 880 substantive student turns for SRL function and help-seeking orientation and related within-session change scores to unaided post-test performance.

article_title: Same Performance, Different Process: Epistemic Ownership in AI-Mediated Education
citation: Jorge Fábrega. (2026). Same Performance, Different Process: Epistemic Ownership in AI-Mediated Education. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02731
title: Epistemic ownership: a four-capacity framework for the learner's command over AI-mediated work
description: Epistemic ownership is an interpretive framework for the learner's justificatory command over work produced through distributed cognition with external systems, including generative AI. It comprises four interdependent functions: "direction, integration, evaluation and answerability". The article uses the first three, which can leave observable traces in AI-mediated interaction, to characterize how cognitive work is distributed between learner and system; answerability requires additional elicitation. The framework also names justificatory dispossession, the condition in which strong performance coexists with weak command because an adequate AI contribution is adopted without the learner reconstructing its reasoning.
requirements: Analysis of observable interaction traces requires sequential interaction records in which learner re-entry after an AI contribution can be examined
constraints: The article states epistemic ownership itself cannot be read directly from a chat transcript; absence of a coded behavior does not establish absence of the underlying capacity, and answerability lies beyond the empirical analysis developed here
target_learners: higher-education students in artificial intelligence and computer science courses
target_learning_goals: learner command over AI-mediated cognitive work
justification and evaluation of AI contributions
examples: The article applies the framework's first three dimensions to 150 StudyChat conversations, coding turn-level evidence of Direction, Integration, and Evaluation
key_sources: Jorge Fábrega. (2026). Same Performance, Different Process: Epistemic Ownership in AI-Mediated Education. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02731

article_title: Guarded adoption of generative AI in higher education: high-achieving students, successful-student identity
citation: Jason Zagami. (2026). Guarded adoption of generative AI in higher education: high-achieving students, successful-student identity, and epistemic agency in a single-university mixed-methods survey. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education 23:47. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00625-6
title: Epistemic agency as the primary frame for evaluating student AI use: the learner's relation to outputs matters more than amount of use
description: The paper adopts epistemic agency (drawing on Nieminen and Ketonen, 2024) as its strongest primary frame, shifting attention "from tool adoption to knowledge positioning". A student may use AI extensively and still exercise strong epistemic agency by treating outputs as provisional, interrogating warrants, verifying claims, and subordinating them to their own judgment; conversely, light use can be weak if outputs are accepted uncritically. The article concludes that "low AI use is not automatically educationally valuable, and high AI use is not automatically suspect". Supporting concepts include possible selves, identity-based motivation, and self-authorship.
requirements: Attention to how students relate to knowledge, assessment, and responsibility, not merely what they know
constraints: The article states the survey measures are not psychometrically strong enough to test a full motivational model, and it cannot claim to observe self-authorship in a formal developmental sense from brief survey comments
target_learning_goals: exercising judgment over AI outputs; remaining a responsible agent in relation to pre-processed information
examples: The article's distinction between a student who interrogates and verifies AI outputs while using them heavily, and one who uses AI lightly but accepts outputs uncritically

article_title: Cognitive Episodes in LLM Reasoning Traces Enable Interpretable Human Item Difficulty Prediction
citation: Chenguang Wang, Ming Li, Xinyue Zeng, Zhuochun Li, Hong Jiao, Tianyi Zhou, Dawei Zhou. (2026). Cognitive Episodes in LLM Reasoning Traces Enable Interpretable Human Item Difficulty Prediction. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.28186
title: Epi2Diff framework: episode-induced process representations combined with semantic embeddings for item difficulty prediction
description: Epi2Diff (Episode to Difficulty) converts model-generated reasoning traces into sentence-level episode sequences and extracts compact features capturing reasoning effort. Its episode-induced process representation "combines three complementary groups of features: length features capturing the overall scale of the reasoning process, episode-distribution features characterizing its composition across episode types, and transition features encoding its local sequential organization". These 83 process features are concatenated with a Sentence-BERT item embedding, averaged across direct, weak, medium, and strong prompting profiles, and fed to a supervised predictor (XGBoost across all datasets). Code is released at the article's GitHub website.
requirements: Access to a reasoning-oriented LLM to generate traces under multiple prompting profiles, and a trained episode-labeling classifier
constraints: The article states the prompting profiles "should not be interpreted as validated simulations of human students or ability levels"

The ethics section states automated predictions must not be the sole basis for test construction, item approval, placement, or licensure decisions, and deployment should include expert review, validation, subgroup fairness analysis, and monitoring for distribution shift
target_learners: Examinees of large-scale assessments (SAT, Cambridge English Qualifications, USMLE) whose items are being calibrated
target_learning_goals: Accurate, interpretable prediction of human item difficulty for test construction and item-quality review
examples: Applied to four benchmarks: USMLE (667 items), Cambridge (793 questions), SAT Reading & Writing (1,338 questions), and SAT Math (1,075 questions)

article_title: The nature of science in the age of generative artificial intelligence: Epistemic authority and materiality
citation: Muminova, Z. O., Mamatkulov, D. M., Turokulova, R. I., Rakhmonova, N. T., Shavqiyev, O. S. O., & Zoirova, S. U. (2026). The nature of science in the age of generative artificial intelligence: Epistemic authority, materiality, and a synergetic response. EURASIA Journal of Mathematics, Science and Technology Education, 22(10), em2943. https://doi.org/10.29333/ejmste/19481
title: Tripartite distinction of epistemic authority: warranted dependence, perceived authority, and uncritical deference
description: The article distinguishes three situations of epistemic reliance to give the concept of epistemic authority more careful handling than it usually receives. "Warranted epistemic dependence refers to justified reliance on a source whose claims can be traced, whose errors can be estimated, and whose authority can be contested." Perceived authority arises from surface features such as fluency, immediacy, and apparent certainty, while uncritical deference suspends any demand for justification. Only the third is at odds with the aims of science education; the identified risk is the slide from the second to the third.
requirements: Vigilance is framed as calibrated trust rather than generalized distrust, compatible with the trust teachers and scientific institutions legitimately command
constraints: The risk identified concerns the slide from perceived authority to uncritical deference, not reliance on sources as such
target_learning_goals: calibrating trust in AI-generated and scientific sources
understanding epistemic authority in science
examples: Cooper (2023) is cited for the risk of a conversational model positioning itself as the ultimate epistemic authority in science education

article_title: The Paternalistic Filter: Epistemic Injustice and Differential Refusal in LLM-Mediated History Education for Marginalized Romanian Students
citation: Alexis Popovici, Andrei Ionascu, Adrian Marius Dumitran. (2026). The Paternalistic Filter: Epistemic Injustice and Differential Refusal in LLM-Mediated History Education for Marginalized Romanian Students. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11292
title: Epistemic paternalism in LLM tutoring as hermeneutical injustice
description: The article's central explanatory framework holds that LLM tutors constitute "epistemic paternalism: withholding civic complexity from marginalized learners while replacing it with victimization-centered narratives." Drawing on Fricker's hermeneutical injustice—a gap in interpretive resources that disadvantages groups in understanding their social experience—the authors argue safety alignment acts as a paternalistic filter transforming conversational AI into "agents of narrative segregation." The framework unifies the audit's four empirical patterns (refusal, gatekeeping, lexical simplification, framing shifts) as one mechanism.
requirements: Requires deployment of LLMs as conversational tutors for politically contested historical content to marginalized learner populations
constraints: Established for a single contested event (the 1989 Romanian Revolution) and single-turn interactions; the authors state future work must verify whether the patterns are universal across other cultural contexts and multi-turn tutoring
target_learners: Marginalized secondary students, including Roma and low socio-economic tier learners
target_learning_goals: Understanding contested national history as political actors with access to interpretive tools and civic agency
examples: The audit operationalized the framework via five metrics: Differential Refusal, Coup Gap, Type-Token Ratio, Agency Theft Ratio, and Mean Justification Scores
key_sources: Alexis Popovici, Andrei Ionascu, Adrian Marius Dumitran. (2026). The Paternalistic Filter: Epistemic Injustice and Differential Refusal in LLM-Mediated History Education for Marginalized Romanian Students. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11292

article_title: Towards Valid Student Simulation with Large Language Models
citation: Zhihao Yuan, Yunze Xiao, Ming Li, Weihao Xuan, Richard Tong, Mona Diab, Tom Mitchell. (2026). Towards Valid Student Simulation with Large Language Models. https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.05473
title: Epistemic State Specification (ESS) with five levels E0–E4
description: ESS is a required system declaration stating what the simulated learner can access at a given moment, how errors are generated, and whether and how the state changes over time. The article operationalizes it as "a lightweight reporting label with five levels", from E0 (unspecified) through E1 static bounded, E2 curriculum-indexed, and E3 misconception-structured, to E4 calibrated or learned against human interaction data. It is intended to prevent overclaiming and enable cross-system comparison.
requirements: Each simulated-student system must explicitly declare its epistemic state specification as a cross-cutting reporting artifact
constraints: The authors note real-world model behaviors often exhibit fluctuating or indeterminate knowledge boundaries, which the E0–E4 taxonomy idealizes for analytical clarity
target_learners: Researchers building and evaluating LLM-based student simulators
target_learning_goals: Falsifiable, auditable claims about simulated learner competence and learning dynamics
examples: Appendix B provides illustrative examples of several ESS levels applied to named systems

article_title: When Youth Enter The Chat: An Epistemic Shift in the Validation of LLM-Based Measures of Student Talk
citation: Liliana Santos-Deonizio, James Malamut, Ramón Antonio Martínez, and Dorottya Demszky. (2027). When Youth Enter The Chat: An Epistemic Shift in the Validation of LLM-Based Measures of Student Talk. In Proceedings of TBD (CSCW '27). ACM, New York, NY, USA. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.23780
title: Two-part epistemic shift in validating LLM-based measures of student talk
description: The article proposes a framework in which validation is treated as a knowledge-production practice shaped by epistemic authority. It argues "language should not be treated solely as a text-based representation, but as a situated, social, cultural, and embodied experience" requiring re-contextualization, and that youth should enter validation as epistemic authorities on their own talk, not merely subjects of expert annotation. The framework draws on epistemic agency, authority, and exclusion constructs, extending them from classroom interaction to the research process itself.
requirements: Youth must be engaged through methods that re-contextualize transcripts, such as participant retrospection and member checks
constraints: The article's participatory engagement was scoped to the validation phase; youth were not involved in designing the coding scheme or LLM prompts
target_learners: multilingual youth in middle school math classrooms
target_learning_goals: valid and equitable measurement of student math talk and collaboration
examples: Figure 1 maps the shift from excluding to including students in the knowledge-production process before and after youth involvement

article_title: Community-Based AI Learning: Redistributing Artificial Intelligence's Epistemic Authority in Education
citation: Santiago Ojeda-Ramirez, Symone Gyles and Kylie Peppler. 2026. Community-Based AI Learning: Redistributing Artificial Intelligence's Epistemic Authority in Education. In Proceedings of 2026 Conference for Research on Equitable and Sustained Participation in Engineering, Computing, and Technology (RESPECT 2026). https://doi.org/10.1145/3796496.3811760
title: Epistemic fine tuning: learner-centered recalibration of trust in AI outputs
description: The paper redefines fine tuning from a technical ML operation into a learner-centered process: "We use the term to describe a learner-centered calibration of how AI outputs are interpreted, trusted, and used when learning is anchored in community concerns." Learners treat AI claims as partial and decontextualized, adjusting confidence by comparing outputs against lived experience, local histories, and community expertise, making trust of AI outputs conditional and context dependent.
requirements: Learners must have access to community-grounded knowledge as an interpretive resource for comparing against AI outputs
constraints: Epistemic fine tuning is not a model adaptation; it adjusts the learner's stance, not the model's parameters
target_learners: Students learning with and about AI in community-anchored settings
target_learning_goals: Conditional, context-dependent trust calibration of AI outputs
examples: A student who knows their neighborhood's economic conditions, food culture, or family history can notice when an AI output describes a place that does not match the place they actually live in, and explain why.

article_title: Faculty Readiness for AI-Supported Teaching and Scalable Online Program Delivery in Higher Education: The EPIQ-AI Framework for Epistemic Integrity
citation: Sangwa, S., Ndahayo, C., Dusengumuremyi, F., & Mutabazi, P. (2025). Faculty Readiness for AI-Supported Teaching and Scalable Online Program Delivery in Higher Education: The EPIQ-AI Framework for Epistemic Integrity. https://doi.org/10.35542/osf.io/kj4vt_v1
title: EPIQ-AI Readiness Framework: readiness as alignment across epistemic, pedagogical, institutional, and quality-and-compliance domains
description: The EPIQ-AI Readiness Framework is the article's principal contribution: a higher-education-specific readiness theory integrating technology acceptance, teacher knowledge (TPACK), and organizational readiness for change traditions. It posits that "credible AI-supported teaching and scalable online delivery require alignment across micro-level faculty capacities and macro-level institutional systems, mediated by pedagogical and assessment design capacity". Readiness is reframed as a sociotechnical and epistemic condition rather than an individual skills deficit, organized into four domains: epistemic, pedagogical, institutional, and quality-and-compliance readiness, operationalized through a dashboard of threshold indicators.
requirements: Alignment across micro-level faculty capacities and macro-level institutional systems, mediated by pedagogical and assessment design capacity
constraints: The framework is derived from secondary sources with different populations and instruments, limiting direct statistical comparability across estimates
target_learning_goals: Credible AI-supported teaching, assessment validity, epistemic integrity, and scalable policy-compliant online program delivery
examples: Table 3 translates the framework into an operational dashboard linking each readiness domain to illustrative indicators and institutional action priorities

article_title: Academic Erasure: The Disappearance of Complexity Under AI-Supported Writing
citation: Chinomso Nwagboso & Sunday Atuba. (2026). Academic erasure: the disappearance of complexity under AI-supported writing. Teaching in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1080/13562517.2026.2707601
title: Epistemic delegation and epistemic singularity as the two mechanisms producing academic erasure
description: The article frames academic erasure as the joint effect of two mechanisms. Epistemic delegation is "the displacement of that labour onto generative AI, the act of handing over the work of thinking to machines optimised for fluency"; the article argues it is structured by design, since AI systems interpolate rather than reason. Epistemic singularity names the homogenisation effect at scale, in which disciplinary, cultural, and individual variation collapses into a dominant AI-optimised register. Together they displace the slow, situated cognitive work writing is meant to support.
requirements: Student access to generative AI tools in high-stakes, time-pressured, or confidence-poor contexts, which the article says makes delegation a rational shortcut
constraints: The article presents this as theoretical framing grounded in educator discourse, not a tested causal model; it notes planned comparative analysis of AI-generated outputs versus pre-AI writing was not undertaken in this study
target_learning_goals: knowledge construction through writing
authorial voice
disciplinary positioning
examples: Students prompting an AI to write an essay bypass the iterative work of formulating arguments, working through tensions, and synthesising sources

title: Electronic Performance Support Systems (EPSSs) as the environment for consulting procedural information
description: The chapter assigns Electronic Performance Support Systems (EPSSs) to the procedural-information component of 4C-ID. The abstract states: "They may consult procedural information in Electronic Performance Support Systems (EPSSs), where principles facilitate a process of knowledge compilation." In this arrangement, EPSSs serve as just-in-time repositories of procedural information that learners consult while working on tasks, with multimedia principles chosen to support knowledge compilation.

target_learning_goals: Knowledge compilation of procedural information

article_title: Investigating Epistemic Stances in Game Play with Data Mining
citation: Martinez-Garza, M. M., & Clark, D. B. (2017). Investigating Epistemic Stances in Game Play with Data Mining. International Journal of Gaming and Computer-Mediated Simulations, 9(3). https://doi.org/10.4018/IJGCMS.2017070101
title: EPIGAME (The Fuzzy Chronicles): a conceptually-integrated puzzle game for Newtonian kinematics with full action logging
description: EPIGAME, titled The Fuzzy Chronicles, is the third iteration of the SURGE line of digital games for Newtonian kinematics, presented as a series of science-fiction puzzles across 32 levels of generally increasing complexity. Students plan a trajectory, place Boost actions at waypoints, and run the attempt; a planning phase plus its action phase form an attempt. The article states it is "intended to help students advance their understanding of Newtonian kinematics" and that the game "stores all student actions and collects them in a central database", enabling log-file analysis.
requirements: Students must have individual computers and the game's central database must record attempt-level parameters for log analysis
constraints: The game neither suggests nor encourages either incremental or whole-plan solution approaches, so students self-select their strategy
target_learning_goals: Newtonian kinematics
force and motion concepts
examples: Study 2 deployed EPIGAME across five consecutive 45-minute class periods with 123 7th grade students

article_title: Rethinking Education in a Changing World
citation: UNESCO Secretariat. (2013). Rethinking Education in a Changing World. UNESCO Education Research and Foresight. https://unesdoc.unesco.org/
title: Recognize and integrate alternative knowledge systems and epistemologies of the South in international education debates
description: The report argues that dominant knowledge is a locus of power and that the Delors report spoke from a Northern epistemic location. It recommends that 'voices from the Global South be heard in current international education debates' and that alternative traditional knowledge systems be recognized rather than relegated to an inferior status. Integration of Southern knowledge, paradigms and visions is presented as a starting point for a paradigm shift regarding knowledge for development.
requirements: Recognition of the relationship of power between knowledge systems in the North and South; avoidance of generalizations about lived realities
constraints: The report notes the Delors report 'neglected the epistemology of the South and spoke in one voice from a single perspective'
target_learners: learners and communities in the Global South and multicultural societies
target_learning_goals: respect for cultural diversity and plural knowledge systems in education
examples: The report cites 'sumak kawsay', the Quechua notion of 'buen vivir' or good living, as an alternative conception of development incorporated into some Andean constitutions

article_title: Learning to think together: Creativity, interdisciplinary collaboration and epistemic control
citation: Gardiner Paul. (2020). Learning to think together: Creativity, interdisciplinary collaboration and epistemic control. Thinking Skills and Creativity. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tsc.2020.100749
title: Framework for epistemic control: a four-stage metacognitive scaffold for collaborative thinking
description: The article proposes a metacognitive framework that scaffolds collaborative thinking on complex problems through four sequential stages: epistemic awareness, epistemic humility, epistemic empathy, and epistemic control. As the abstract states, "Moving from epistemic awareness, through epistemic humility and epistemic empathy, students develop epistemic control." The framework aims to develop students' metacognitive understanding and epistemic awareness to enable epistemic shifting, perspective taking and cross-disciplinary communication, and is summarised in Fig. 1.
requirements: Students first actively reflect on their own disciplinary knowledge tradition, its products and processes, before later stages can develop
constraints: The article presents the framework as a proposal and calls for further research into its benefits across learning contexts; no empirical test of the framework is reported
target_learning_goals: collaborative creative problem solving on complex problems
interdisciplinary perspective taking and knowledge integration
examples: The framework is presented as a scaffold for individuals working on complex real-world problems in diverse collaborative groups, summarised in Fig. 1

article_title: Learning to think together: Creativity, interdisciplinary collaboration and epistemic control
citation: Gardiner Paul. (2020). Learning to think together: Creativity, interdisciplinary collaboration and epistemic control. Thinking Skills and Creativity. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tsc.2020.100749
title: Epistemic games and forms: disciplines as rule-governed knowledge-making cultures
description: Drawing on Collins and Ferguson (1993), the article frames each discipline as an 'epistemic culture' with a set of rules and strategies: "Each discipline culture has a set of rules and strategies, called epistemic games, that constrain inquiry and target structures." Epistemic games are the mental processes that make knowledge; epistemic forms are the means of communicating and representing inquiry findings. Students are asked 'what do you do in your discipline?' and 'What does that action produce?' to surface their discipline's games and forms, developing domain meta-knowledge that supports creativity within the domain.
requirements: Students need strong understanding of their own domain for epistemic awareness to develop from within it
constraints: The article notes the more disciplines evolve, the more complex and constrained the games and forms become
target_learners: secondary and tertiary students working in disciplinary and interdisciplinary contexts
target_learning_goals: understanding the strengths and limits of one's own way of knowing
domain meta-knowledge supporting disciplinary creativity
examples: Mastering these games and forms grants the learner access to the discipline's community of practice, per Markauskaite and Goodyear (2017)

article_title: Student Behavior and Epistemological Framing: Examples from Collaborative Active-Learning Activities in Physics
citation: Rachel E. Scherr and David Hammer. (2007). Student Behavior and Epistemological Framing: Examples from Collaborative Active-Learning Activities in Physics. Submitted to Cognition and Instruction. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Student+Behavior+and+Epistemological+Framing
title: Epistemological framing as a resource-based, dynamic-systems account of student sense of an activity
description: The article develops epistemological framing from anthropology and linguistics: to frame a situation is to interpret it based on previous experience, bringing expectations about what could happen and what action is appropriate. In school settings, students form "a sense of what is taking place with respect to knowledge." Building on a resource model, a frame is "a locally coherent pattern of activations" that may span individuals or a group, linking discourse dynamics with models of individual cognition.
requirements: Analysis requires observable verbal, paraverbal, and nonverbal contextualizing cues in social interaction, since frames emerge in and are constituted by interaction
constraints: Frames are local: the coherence may be particular to the moment or context, so identified framings are local shifts within larger framings of a session
target_learners: introductory university physics students working in small collaborative groups
target_learning_goals: students' understanding of knowledge, reasoning, and learning in physics (epistemological framing of instructional activities)
examples: Jasmin's singsong reading from the worksheet versus her loud, pointing commentary on it, recognized by her peer Sheryl

article_title: Making Space to Sensemake: Epistemic Distancing in Small Group Physics Discussions
citation: Conlin, L. D., & Scherr, R. E. (2012). Making Space to Sensemake: Epistemic Distancing in Small Group Physics Discussions. Preprint under review. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Making+Space+to+Sensemake
title: Epistemic distancing as a discursive resource for managing epistemological and affective dynamics
description: Epistemic distancing is defined as "any discourse move by which a participant in conversation downgrades their epistemic stance, for example by hedging, quoting, or joking." It is "epistemic" because it concerns the speaker's commitment to truth, and "distancing" because it creates distance between speaker and claim, protecting affect if the idea is evaluated negatively. The article uses it to explain how tutorial groups co-construct safe spaces for sensemaking, drawing on research on stance-taking and footing shifts.
requirements: Face-to-face collaborative discussion in which ideas are shared and critiqued, where affective risk of rejection exists
constraints: More distancing is not necessarily better; over-distancing can lead groups to avoid conflict or dismiss the activity
target_learners: undergraduate physics students in inquiry-based tutorials
target_learning_goals: collaborative scientific sensemaking about physical mechanisms
examples: Deirdre phrases disagreement about the normal force's direction as a question; Bree reads her written answer with ironic sing-song prosody

article_title: Bringing maker practices to school: tracing discursive and materially mediated aspects of student teams’ collaborative making processes
citation: Riikonen, S., Seitamaa-Hakkarainen, P., & Hakkarainen, K. (2020). Bringing maker practices to school: tracing discursive and materially mediated aspects of student teams' collaborative making processes. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-020-09330-6
title: Epistemic-object account of collaborative making
description: The article frames collaborative making through the construct of epistemic objects: "Epistemic objects are envisioned as well as future-oriented invention ideas, which are characterized by their incompleteness and infinite potential for improvement through sustained iterative efforts." Pursuing such an incompletely specified object keeps a team's discussion, sketching, prototyping and experimentation aligned, and material artifacts such as sketches and prototypes serve as anchors that make vague ideas discussable and force convergence toward shared understanding. The account underpins the authors' explanation of which teams succeeded.
requirements: teams must jointly regulate activity toward the object rather than work on disconnected individual tasks
constraints: the process is emergent and nonlinear, so goals, tools and products cannot be pre-determined, which makes teacher scaffolding challenging
target_learners: adolescent students in teams doing open-ended co-invention challenges
target_learning_goals: co-inventing artifacts
knowledge-creating learning
examples: Bike and MGG shared their epistemic objects and refined them through experimentation and model making across the project, whereas the Plant team generated no such object.

article_title: Socio-technical configurations for productive talk
citation: Peter Reimann. (2021). Socio-technical configurations for productive talk. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn (2021) 16:301–306. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-021-09354-6
title: Epistemic Network Analysis reveals temporally ordered patterns in sequentially produced coded data
description: The article describes ENA as an extension of bag-of-words text-mining that adds a sliding time "window" so co-occurrences are counted over meaningful parts of text, called "stanzas". Coded data form the nodes of a transition graph with co-occurrences as edges, allowing graph features and network visualization. The article states that "ENA allows the researcher to reveal temporally ordered patterns in sequentially produced data" and that it enabled nuanced condition differences and a better understanding of Simple questions' roles in talk.
requirements: Input data are coded in some high-level coding framework, such as teacher actions (7 codes) or student dyad interactions (9 categories), as the article describes.
target_learners: collaborative learners in classrooms and pair-programming settings, including students and teachers
target_learning_goals: understanding and explaining patterns of productive collaborative talk and interaction
examples: Amarasinghe and colleagues used ENA to find nuanced differences between mirroring and guidance dashboard conditions; Vandenberg and colleagues used it to understand the different roles Simple questions played.

article_title: Socio-technical configurations for productive talk
citation: Peter Reimann. (2021). Socio-technical configurations for productive talk. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn (2021) 16:301–306. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-021-09354-6
title: Task epistemic complexity drives the tension between epistemic and social attention in orchestration
description: Because the study's epistemic artefacts "were not simple yes/no answers, but rather solutions to programming problems", teachers had to invest considerable effort in appraising them, which in the mirroring condition shifted attention toward epistemic rather than social aspects. Designers of collaboration support should therefore anticipate that the effort required to appraise student artefacts consumes orchestration capacity that would otherwise go to social interaction. The article treats this as a genuine tension revealed by the data.
requirements: Teachers need cognitive resources for appraising complex epistemic artefacts; tools should reduce this load (e.g., guidance dashboards) to keep attention balanced.
constraints: The interpretation that the guidance condition balances attention is tentative due to the small sample and absence of learning outcome measures.
target_learners: teachers orchestrating synchronous group work in classrooms
target_learning_goals: balancing attention to epistemic and social aspects of student collaboration
examples: In the six-teacher dashboard study, a variant of the pyramid collaboration script was enacted on individual, group, and class levels with students voting on the quality of programming solutions.

article_title: Knowledge creation through maker practices and the role of teacher and peer support in collaborative invention projects
citation: Sini Davies, Pirita Seitamaa-Hakkarainen, Kai Hakkarainen. (2024). Knowledge creation through maker practices and the role of teacher and peer support in collaborative invention projects. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09427-2
title: Epistemic objects as emergent, evolving invention-in-making guiding co-invention
description: Epistemic objects are the emergent envisioned solutions or inventions-in-making that guide and mediate knowledge-creating learning, anchored in science and technology studies. They comprise "the intertwined epistemic and material aspects of design" instantiated in sketches and prototypes, crystallize what participants seek to accomplish and do not yet know, and remain evolving and open to interpretation, actively inviting team members' contributions by raising new questions.
requirements: A shared, deliberately under-refined invention object that team members can interpret and contribute to jointly
constraints: Highly refined digital design artifacts such as CAD models "can be problematic in terms of functioning as epistemic objects and may limit experimentation owing to their high refinement and apparent accuracy"
target_learners: lower-secondary students (13-14 years old) in maker-centered STEAM projects
target_learning_goals: knowledge creation through collaboratively inventing and making materially embodied artifacts
examples: The three analyzed teams each maintained a shared epistemic object (an automated button presser, a smart sleep pillow, a solar power bank), conveying ideas through sketches and prototypes

article_title: Examining my-side bias during and after reading controversial historical accounts
citation: Iordanou, K., Kendeou, P., & Zembylas, M. (2020). Examining my-side bias during and after reading controversial historical accounts. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-020-09240-w
title: Kuhn et al.'s developmental theory of epistemic cognition: absolutist, multiplist, and evaluativist levels
description: The article organizes individual differences in epistemic beliefs using Kuhn et al.'s (2000) theory of epistemic development, in which "epistemic cognition progresses from the absolutist level, to the multiplist level and then to the evaluativist level". At the absolutist level knowledge is objective and certain; at the multiplist level it is subjective and uncertain; at the evaluativist level a balance is achieved and the position "better supported by argument and evidence" is judged to have more merit. The study used this framework to classify participants via the Livia problem and to predict my-side bias and epistemic processing.
requirements: Assessment instrument that distinguishes responses about rightness of accounts and certainty of knowledge, such as the Livia problem used in the study
constraints: The article notes knowledge of epistemic beliefs in the domain of history is very limited and based mainly on inferences rather than direct empirical evidence
target_learning_goals: critical evaluation of contradictory historical accounts
epistemic cognition about knowledge and knowing
examples: Participants were classified as absolutist, multiplist, or evaluativist based on their Livia problem responses; nine were evaluativists and 30 were absolutist or multiplist

article_title: Supporting strategic and meta-strategic development of argument skill: the role of reflection
citation: Iordanou, K. (2022). Supporting strategic and meta-strategic development of argument skill: the role of reflection. Metacognition and Learning, 17, 399–425. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-021-09289-1
title: Three developmental levels of epistemic understanding: Absolutism, Multiplism, and Evaluativism
description: The article describes epistemic understanding as developing through three levels across the lifespan. "The first developmental level of epistemic understanding is Absolutism", where truth is objective and disagreeing claims are dismissed as false beliefs. "Multiplism is the second developmental level", acknowledging that knowledge is subjective and multiple interpretations may exist, so disagreeing parties see no point in discussion. "The final level of development is the Evaluativist level, where the subjective and objective dimensions of knowing are coordinated": knowledge is judgment formed by evaluating alternatives against evidence, and argumentation is valued as a means of evaluating knowledge claims.
requirements: Opportunities to engage in practice in dialogic argumentation and reflection while arguing, over an extended period of time, for development toward evaluativist understanding
constraints: The article states epistemic understanding undergoes development throughout the lifespan and its roots trace to early conceptions of evidence as objective reality
target_learners: children through adults, with the levels illustrated for adolescents in argumentation contexts
target_learning_goals: epistemic understanding of the nature of knowledge and evidence; disposition to engage in argumentation
examples: The article links evaluativist understanding to a mindset of searching for more evidence and considering alternative interpretive frameworks before making a judgment

article_title: How Mathematicians Obtain Conviction: Implications for Mathematics Instruction and Research on Epistemic Cognition
citation: Keith Weber, Matthew Inglis & Juan Pablo Mejia-Ramos. (2013). How mathematicians obtain conviction: Implications for mathematics instruction and research on epistemic cognition. https://dspace.lboro.ac.uk/
title: Epistemic aims framework for mathematical conviction
description: The article adopts the construct of epistemic aims—"goals related to finding things out, understanding them, and forming beliefs"—and argues that the sources of evidence mathematicians use depend on which aim they pursue. It distinguishes four aims: convincing oneself an assertion is true, producing a peer-sanctioned deductive proof, verifying a proof's correctness, and increasing understanding of the mathematics behind the assertion. The framework underpins the paper's argument that empirical or authoritarian evidence can rationally persuade for some aims while deductive evidence is needed for understanding-generating learning opportunities.
requirements: Research on justification must distinguish the epistemic aim a person pursues, since different aims license different types of evidence
constraints: A full account of the understanding aim is beyond the scope of the paper, which treats understanding as explanation, new methods, new relationships, and new representations via cited sources
target_learning_goals: justifying mathematical assertions
gaining conviction in mathematical claims
understanding why theorems are true
examples: The paper uses the four aims to reinterpret studies of students' empirical justifications, arguing the studies did not establish which aim students pursued
key_sources: Keith Weber, Matthew Inglis & Juan Pablo Mejia-Ramos. (2013). How mathematicians obtain conviction: Implications for mathematics instruction and research on epistemic cognition. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2013.865527

article_title: Moving Beyond Reflection: Reflexivity and Epistemic Cognition in Teaching and Teacher Education
citation: Feucht, F. C., Lunn Brownlee, J., & Schraw, G. (2017). Moving beyond reflection: Reflexivity and epistemic cognition in teaching and teacher education. Educational Psychologist, 52(4), 234-241. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2017.1350180
title: The epistemic climate construct and the Educational Model for Personal Epistemology
description: The epistemic climate construct (Bendixen & Rule; Feucht; Muis & Duffy) provides the broader classroom context for the 3R-EC Framework. The Educational Model for Personal Epistemology (Feucht, 2010a) describes how the nature of knowledge and knowing emerge from epistemic entities in classrooms: 'the epistemic cognition of learners and teachers, the epistemic underpinning of instruction ... and of educational materials ... and the reciprocal relations among these entities'. The model was developed to account for changes in epistemic climate across context, culture and time, and its entities can become the targeted focus of self-reflection leading to epistemic reflexivity.
requirements: Application requires attention to the reciprocal relations among learner cognition, teacher cognition, instruction and materials rather than any single entity
constraints: The model was developed for classroom settings and extended to cross-context, cross-culture and cross-time comparison
target_learning_goals: awareness of epistemic aspects of learning and instruction
aligning instructional approaches and materials with epistemic cognition
examples: The article proposes that these epistemic entities and their relations 'can be incorporated into the process of self-reflection that lead to epistemic reflexivity in the classroom setting'
key_sources: Feucht, F. C., Lunn Brownlee, J., & Schraw, G. (2017). Moving beyond reflection: Reflexivity and epistemic cognition in teaching and teacher education. Educational Psychologist, 52(4), 234-241. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2017.1350180

article_title: Changing Teachers' Epistemic Cognition: A New Conceptual Framework for Epistemic Reflexivity
citation: Jo Lunn Brownlee, Leila E. Ferguson & Mary Ryan (2017). Changing Teachers' Epistemic Cognition: A New Conceptual Framework for Epistemic Reflexivity. Educational Psychologist, 52(4), 242–252. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2017.1333430
title: Epistemic reflexivity extends reflection by adding internal dialogue evaluating multiple perspectives and leading to action
description: Drawing on Archer and on Ryan and Bourke, the article distinguishes reflection from reflexivity. Reflection is treated as a necessary component of reflexivity, but reflexivity adds an internal dialogue that evaluates multiple perspectives — the individual's and those situated in the broader social context — and maintains or changes courses of action. Reflexivity is characterized by discernment (reflecting on a key issue or aim), deliberation (weighing personal and contextual concerns), and dedication (resolved action). The article argues this distinction matters because metacognitive thinking strategies alone fail to account for changes in learning behavior.
requirements: Internal dialogue that evaluates multiple perspectives including school policies, curriculum expectations, and social justice agendas
Deliberative action following reflective thought
constraints: Reflexivity is described as always situated and potentially transformative, so its impact depends on the immediate and broader political and social context
target_learning_goals: Changing epistemic cognition for teaching practice
Moving from reflection to resolved action in classrooms
examples: Ryan and Bourke's account of reflexivity as bending-back thought upon self, taking the form of subject-object-subject, is used to frame teachers' deliberation about teaching to the test versus student well-being
key_sources: Jo Lunn Brownlee, Leila E. Ferguson & Mary Ryan (2017). Changing Teachers' Epistemic Cognition: A New Conceptual Framework for Epistemic Reflexivity. Educational Psychologist, 52(4), 242–252. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2017.1333430

article_title: Teachers' Epistemic Cognition in Classroom Assessment
citation: Fives, Helenrose, Barnes, Nicole, Buehl, Michelle, Mascadri, Julia, & Ziegler, Nathan. (2017). Teachers’ epistemic cognition in classroom assessment. Educational Psychologist, 52(4), pp. 270-283. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2017.1323218
title: Model of epistemic cognition in teaching embedded in pedagogical decision making
description: The article presents a nested model situating teachers' epistemic cognition within pedagogical decision making situated in the task of teaching, informed by domain knowledge and the teacher's self-system. It comprises epistemic aims, reliable processes, and consideration and evaluation of epistemic matters, producing epistemically informed praxis. The authors state: "Figure 1 provides a model of epistemic cognition in teaching informed by the work of Buehl and Fives (2016), Chinn et al. (2011, 2014), and Greene et al. (2008)." The process is iterative rather than linear in practice.
requirements: Epistemic cognition is only invoked when pedagogical decision making is knowledge focused, relating to the construction, use, or justification of knowledge
constraints: The authors note the process "visually depicted and described here as linear, in practice is more recursive, iterative, and multi-directional"
target_learning_goals: teachers' epistemic cognition in planning, constructing, and using classroom assessment events
examples: A hypothetical educational psychology instructor, Dr. Jones, works through the model while assessing students' understanding of learning theories
key_sources: Fives, Helenrose, Barnes, Nicole, Buehl, Michelle, Mascadri, Julia, & Ziegler, Nathan. (2017). Teachers’ epistemic cognition in classroom assessment. Educational Psychologist, 52(4), pp. 270-283. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2017.1323218

article_title: Self-regulated learning processes vary as a function of epistemic beliefs and contexts: Mixed method evidence from eye tracking and concurrent and retrospective reports
citation: Gregory Trevors, Reza Feyzi-Behnagh, Roger Azevedo, François Bouchet. Self-Regulated Learning Processes Vary as a Function of Epistemic Beliefs and Contexts: Mixed Method Evidence from Eye Tracking and Concurrent and Retrospective Reports. Learning and Instruction, 2016, 42, pp.31-46. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2015.11.003
title: Epistemic cognition as a determinant of phase- and component-specific self-regulated learning under varying learning conditions
description: The article frames epistemic cognition as related to "specific phases and components of self-regulated learning and its adaptation to learning conditions of varying quality." In this account, learners' beliefs about knowledge interact with the quality of learning conditions: when science content relays conceptual discrepancies, learners' epistemic cognition shapes how they behaviorally process, notice, and resolve the discrepancies across SRL phases. The framework is instantiated empirically through eye tracking, study times, metacognitive ratings, think-aloud protocols, and retrospective interviews.
requirements: Learners must encounter science content that relays conceptual discrepancies for the epistemic-cognition-driven adaptation to be observable
constraints: Evidence reported is from university students in science content contexts
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning of science content involving conceptual discrepancies
epistemic cognition and evaluation of conflicting knowledge
examples: Study 1 collected eye tracking patterns, study times, and metacognitive ratings while students processed discrepant science content; Study 2 added concurrent and retrospective verbal reports.
key_sources: Gregory Trevors, Reza Feyzi-Behnagh, Roger Azevedo, François Bouchet. Self-Regulated Learning Processes Vary as a Function of Epistemic Beliefs and Contexts: Mixed Method Evidence from Eye Tracking and Concurrent and Retrospective Reports. article_title: The differential development of epistemic beliefs in psychology and computer science students: A four-wave longitudinal study
citation: Rosman, T., Mayer, A.-K., Kerwer, M., & Krampen, G. (2019). The differential development of epistemic beliefs in psychology and computer science students: A four-wave longitudinal study. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2017.01.006
title: Epistemic sophistication as flexible adaptation of epistemic judgments to specific contexts, not a generalized developmental sequence
description: This account reconceives epistemic 'sophistication' as, in the authors' words, "a flexible adaptation of epistemic judgments to the characteristics of specific contexts, and not as a generalized developmental sequence." It emerged from the finding that belief trajectories diverged by discipline: absolute beliefs increased in computer science while multiplistic beliefs in psychology rose and then steeply decreased. The framework implies that domain context shapes which belief changes count as developmentally advanced.
requirements: Learning contexts must have discernible discipline-specific characteristics of knowledge to which epistemic judgments can adapt.
constraints: Derived from a single four-wave study of undergraduates in two disciplines (computer science and psychology).
target_learning_goals: development of discipline-appropriate epistemic beliefs about the nature of knowledge
examples: The authors suggest the account after observing divergent belief trajectories across the two disciplines in their longitudinal data.
key_sources: Rosman, T., Mayer, A.-K., Kerwer, M., & Krampen, G. (2019). The differential development of epistemic beliefs in psychology and computer science students: A four-wave longitudinal study. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2017.01.006

article_title: Mastery and performance goals predict epistemic and relational conflict regulation.
citation: Darnon, C., Muller, D., Schrager, S. M., Pannuzzo, N., & Butera, F. (2006). Mastery and Performance Goals Predict Epistemic and Relational Conflict Regulation. Journal of Educational Psychology, 98(4), 766–776. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-0663.98.4.766
title: Sociocognitive conflict regulation framework: epistemic versus relational modes
description: The article builds on the sociocognitive conflict framework, in which disagreement between collaborators carries both a cognitive component (doubt about the task content) and a social component (doubt about relative competence). It specifies two modes of regulation: "epistemic regulation, which is focused on task understanding and examination of the validity of each proposition", and relational regulation, which defends one's own competence by affirming one's point of view. The article contributes by linking these modes, previously inferred from influence outcomes, to mastery and performance goals and by showing they can be measured directly or via competence attributions.
requirements: A sociocognitive conflict situation in which a partner's disagreement is credible and plausible, as induced by the prerecorded incorrect but plausible partner answers in Study 2
constraints: Regulation here is not conflict resolution: regulating a conflict in either mode does not necessarily imply the conflict is terminated
Only the approach form of performance goals was examined
target_learning_goals: regulating disagreement over academic material to support understanding
examples: Study 2 induced real sociocognitive conflict by sending participants prerecorded incorrect but plausible partner answers in a computer-mediated cooperative task
Study 1 assessed regulation via direct self-report items such as trying to examine the conditions under which each point of view could help understanding
key_sources: Darnon, C., Muller, D., Schrager, S. M., Pannuzzo, N., & Butera, F. (2006). Mastery and Performance Goals Predict Epistemic and Relational Conflict Regulation. Journal of Educational Psychology, 98(4), 766–776. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-0663.98.4.766

article_title:
Preservice teachers’ epistemic and achievement emotions when
                        confronted with common misconceptions about education.
citation: Berweger, B., Kracke, B., & Dietrich, J. (2023). Preservice Teachers' Epistemic and Achievement Emotions When Confronted With Common Misconceptions About Education. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000792
title: Epistemic versus achievement emotions distinguished by object focus, with epistemic emotions arising from information-oriented appraisals of cognitive incongruity
description: The article organizes learning-related emotions by their object focus, drawing on Pekrun's control-value theory and Muis et al.'s account of epistemic emotions. Epistemic emotions (surprise, curiosity, confusion, and enjoyment, frustration, anxiety when knowledge-focused) "result from information-oriented appraisals about the (mis-)alignment between new information and existing knowledge structures," and motivate critical reflection and exploration. Achievement emotions (anger, pride) are tied to success or failure outcomes. The study operationalizes this distinction by measuring state-level emotions after feedback on misconception statements.
requirements: Requires in-the-moment (state-level) measurement across multiple occasions per person, since the framework concerns intra-individual appraisal-emotion links rather than trait differences.
constraints: The same emotion (e.g., anxiety) belongs to different categories depending on the object focus of attention, so category membership is context-dependent, as the article states.
target_learners: preservice teachers in teacher education programs
target_learning_goals: revising faulty educational knowledge and misconceptions
engaging in evidence-based knowledge exploration
examples: Participants judged 15 misconception statements about class size, grade retention, and direct instruction, received refutational or confirming feedback, rated eight emotions, and could request explanations to resolve discrepancies.
key_sources: Berweger, B., Kracke, B., & Dietrich, J. (2023). Preservice Teachers' Epistemic and Achievement Emotions When Confronted With Common Misconceptions About Education. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000792

article_title: A practical implementation science framework for education
citation: Allen, S. E., Bardach, L., Jirout, J., Mackey, A., McCoy, D., Pesando, L. M., & Kizilcec, R. F. (2026). A practical implementation science framework for education. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00430-w
title: A four-phase implementation framework for education adapted from the EPIS Framework
description: The article presents a simplified protocol for implementing evidence-based pedagogical practices and technologies in real-world educational settings. It breaks the process into four milestones, each of which must be fully met before advancing: "Exploration Phase: Selecting the right intervention requires forming partnerships with students and teachers"; a Preparation Phase for developing a revisable Theory of Change; an Implementation Phase of small-scale testing; and a Sustainment Phase assimilating the intervention into regular operations. The authors chose the EPIS delineation because "it has two planning phases, one for exploration and another for preparation, whereas other process-based frameworks have only one planning phase."
requirements: Each milestone must be achieved and evaluated before moving to the next, using the supplementary checklist to evaluate progress
Successful implementation requires a level of time-consuming, resource-intensive planning that exceeds what can be expected in advance of submitting most grant proposals
constraints: The framework is a simplification: the supplementary tools do not include a list of every factor to consider, and the authors state the protocols should be viewed as a foundation rather than a definitive or exhaustive manual
target_learners: School students in K-12 and higher education settings where evidence-based practices and technologies are being implemented
target_learning_goals: Improving learning outcomes and student well-being through faithful implementation of research-validated pedagogical practices and technologies
examples: The four phases are mapped onto the Milpitas School District technology initiative, which used small-scale pilot tests and ongoing feedback as part of regular operations
key_sources: Allen, S. E., Bardach, L., Jirout, J., Mackey, A., McCoy, D., Pesando, L. M., & Kizilcec, R. F. (2026). A practical implementation science framework for education. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00430-w

article_title: Coordinating the Complexity of Tools, Tasks, and Users: On Theory-based Approaches to Authoring Tool Usability
citation: Tom Murray. (2015). Coordinating the Complexity of Tools, Tasks, and Users: On Theory-based Approaches to Authoring Tool Usability. Int J Artif Intell Educ 26:37–71. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0076-6
title: Epistemic Forms and Games as complexity classes of authoring interface features
description: Drawing on Collins and Ferguson, the article uses Epistemic Forms (and Epistemic Games) to classify authoring tool interface components and procedures into epistemic classes that can be roughly ordered by complexity. As the article puts it, "filling in a text form or setting a slider level are examples of simple tasks, while filling in a table or hierarchy have medium complexity, and creating and debugging formal procedures has much complexity". These classes partially address the dimensionality problem of combining different complexity types into a holistic assessment.
requirements: Tool features must be classifiable into epistemic classes so they can be matched to user complexity capacity
constraints: The article states that Epistemic Forms only partially solves the dimensionality (apples vs. oranges) challenge of integrating various types of complexity
target_learning_goals: ordering authoring tasks and interface features by cognitive complexity

article_title: Improving workplace-based assessment and feedback by an E-portfolio enhanced with learning analytics
citation: van der Schaaf, M., Donkers, J., Slof, B., Moonen-van Loon, J., van Tartwijk, J., Driessen, E., Badii, A., Serban, O., Ten Cate, O. (2016). Improving workplace-based assessment and feedback by an E-portfolio enhanced with learning analytics. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-016-9496-8
title: Entrustable professional activities (EPAs) with five entrustment levels as assessment anchor
description: Workplace-related tasks are operationalized as units of professional practice: "These so-called entrustable professional activities (EPAs) appeared to provide a valid and useful anchor for assessment of learners in medical education-training programs." EPAs are independently executable within a time frame, observable and measurable in process and outcome, making them suitable for entrustment decisions. Learners send competency requests per EPA; supervisors rate entrustment on five levels, from not allowed to practice (level 1) to being able to give the supervision task (level 5), with level four equating to the graduation requirement. EPAs are mapped against competency domains (e.g., CanMEDS roles) via job analysis.
requirements: Roles and competencies must first be developed per workplace-domain, and per domain assessment tools selected and developed, before the E-portfolio can be enhanced
constraints: In medical curricula, EPAs are interrelated: some EPAs are more important in some clerkships or not assessed at all, so entrustment scores in one clerkship can affect scores in another
target_learners: learners in medical, veterinary and teacher education training programs
target_learning_goals: professional competency development and readiness for unsupervised practice
examples: Table 1 maps example EPAs such as consulting new ambulatory patients and leading an in-patient ward against six competency domains
