article_title: Supporting interdisciplinary collaborative concept mapping with individual preparation phase
citation: Esther Tan, Jacob Gerolf de Weerd, Slavi Stoyanov. (2021). Supporting interdisciplinary collaborative concept mapping with individual preparation phase. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-09963-w
title: Epistemic and social process framework for collaborative knowledge co-construction and transactivity
description: The article organises collaborative knowledge co-construction along two dimensions. The epistemic dimension uses Beers et al.'s (2006) 'primitives of negotiation' — contribution, clarification, verification, elaboration — plus the authors' added positioning. The social dimension uses Weinberger and Fischer's (2006) five social modes: "externalisation, elicitation, quick-consensus building, integration-oriented consensus building and conflict-oriented consensus building", which represent different levels of transactivity, with conflict-oriented consensus building the highest. The study applies this framework as coding schemes to audio-recorded collaborative discourse.
requirements: Discourse data coded by trained independent raters with sufficient inter-rater reliability (Cohen's Kappa κ = 0.79 epistemic, κ = 0.88 social)
constraints: Transactivity levels are inferred from nominal-level coded discourse categories rather than direct measures
target_learners: third-year university students in interdisciplinary minors
target_learning_goals: interdisciplinary knowledge integration
collaborative knowledge co-construction
examples: Audio recordings of eight groups' collaborative concept mapping were coded into the epistemic categories and the five social modes, then compared across WIP and WOIP with chi-square tests.
key_sources: Esther Tan, Jacob Gerolf de Weerd, Slavi Stoyanov. (2021). Supporting interdisciplinary collaborative concept mapping with individual preparation phase. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-09963-w

article_title: Refining qualitative ethnographies using Epistemic Network Analysis: A study of socioemotional learning dimensions in a Humanistic Knowledge Building Community
citation: Hod, Yotam; Eagan, Brendan; Katz, Shir. (2020). Refining qualitative ethnographies using Epistemic Network Analysis: A study of socioemotional learning dimensions in a humanistic knowledge building community. Journal article. https://zenodo.org
title: Epistemic Network Analysis as a methodology for producing quantitative ethnographies of complex learning environments
description: Epistemic Network Analysis (ENA) is described as "a methodology for producing quantitative ethnographies based on complex learning environments." The study uses ENA to analyze data collected during a semester of studies in a classroom learning community, applying it to socioemotional facets of learning, which the article notes ENA "has only begun to examine." ENA is positioned as complementary to deep, qualitative ethnography rather than a replacement for it.
requirements: Data collected from a complex learning environment over time, as in the semester of studies analyzed here
constraints: The article states ENA has only begun to examine socioemotional facets of learning in classrooms
target_learning_goals: socioemotional dimensions of learning
sociocognitive development in knowledge building communities
examples: The authors employed ENA to analyze a semester of data from a humanistic knowledge building community, in parallel with a stage developmental qualitative analysis.

article_title: Factors influencing the incorporation of Entrustable Professional Activities into assessment in nutrition and dietetics education: A systematic review.
citation: Surace R, Palermo C, Porter J. (2025). Factors influencing the incorporation of Entrustable Professional Activities into assessment in nutrition and dietetics education: A systematic review. Nutrition & Dietetics. https://doi.org/10.1111/1747-0080.70004
title: EPAs as a tool to support shared understanding and simplicity of judgments in competency-based assessment.
description: The review frames EPAs not as the definitive solution to the complexity of competency-based assessment but rather as a tool to support a shared understanding and simplicity of judgments. EPAs show promise in supporting the untangling of complex CBA by offering a practical, clearly visible, and easily understood authentic form of assessment for assessors and learners, which is outcomes-based and complements existing competency frameworks.
requirements: Linkage to existing competency frameworks.
constraints: EPAs should not be considered the definitive solution to the complexity of competency-based assessment.
target_learning_goals: work-readiness assessment

article_title: Interventions to improve pharmacists' competency in chronic disease management: a systematic review of randomized controlled trials.
citation: Rendrayani Farida, Utami Auliasari M., Insani Widya N., Puspita Falerina, Alfian Sofa D., Nguyen Thang, Puspitasari Irma M. (2024). Interventions to improve pharmacists’ competency in chronic disease management: a systematic review of randomized controlled trials. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06393-z
title: EPOC taxonomy of intervention types for classifying health-professional competency interventions
description: The Cochrane Effective Practice and Organization of Care (EPOC) taxonomy classifies health-system interventions into four types. The review states: "Using the latest EPOC taxonomy [37], the interventions were further categorized into four types" — delivery arrangements, financial arrangements, governance arrangements, and implementation strategies — and uses it to organize its synthesis, arguing the taxonomy "ensures consistent classification and comparability" for decision-makers. In the included studies only implementation strategies and combined implementation strategies–delivery arrangements types appeared.
requirements: Interventions must be classifiable into one of the four EPOC types for consistent classification and comparability
constraints: No financial arrangements or governance arrangements interventions appeared among the 11 included RCTs
target_learners: pharmacists in community and hospital settings
target_learning_goals: knowledge, skills, and attitudes for chronic disease management
examples: The review classified all 11 included RCTs as implementation strategies (n = 8) or combined implementation strategies–delivery arrangements (n = 3)

article_title: Using an e-Portfolio System to Improve the Academic Writing Performance of ESL Students
citation: Ali Alshahrani and Scott Windeatt. (2012). Using an e-Portfolio System to Improve the Academic Writing Performance of ESL Students. EUROCALL Conference, Gothenburg, Sweden, Proceedings. https://research-publishing.net
title: E-portfolio-supported process writing with peer and teacher feedback
description: The pattern uses a web-based e-portfolio system (TaskStream) as a framework within which ESL students work through the key phases of the writing process — pre-writing, drafting and revising — while writing for an audience of peers. The system "allowed learners to write for an audience (each other) and to give feedback to, and receive feedback from, both their intended audience, and their teacher". It aims to develop self-consistency, positive writing self-belief, and realistic self-judgement of strengths and weaknesses as writers.
requirements: Appropriate, regular feedback from peers and the teacher while learners work through planning, drafting and revising stages
A web-based e-portfolio system through which essays are submitted and feedback exchanged
constraints: The article notes e-portfolio use will probably increase the length of time required to cover the curriculum
target_learners: ESL students on intensive English language writing courses
target_learning_goals: Academic writing performance
Writing self-efficacy and self-belief
Consistent application of the writing process approach
examples: 46 ESL students from an English language centre were divided into a conventional group and an experimental e-portfolio group and submitted a series of essays over a number of weeks, receiving peer and teacher feedback
key_sources: Ali Alshahrani and Scott Windeatt. (2012). Using an e-Portfolio System to Improve the Academic Writing Performance of ESL Students. EUROCALL Conference, Gothenburg, Sweden, Proceedings. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED574901

article_title: Using an e-Portfolio System to Improve the Academic Writing Performance of ESL Students
citation: Ali Alshahrani and Scott Windeatt. (2012). Using an e-Portfolio System to Improve the Academic Writing Performance of ESL Students. EUROCALL Conference, Gothenburg, Sweden, Proceedings. https://research-publishing.net
title: Use e-portfolios to give learners control of goal-setting, identity presentation and progress monitoring in writing courses
description: The article argues e-portfolios benefit learners by letting them "control their learning by setting their own learning goals and the time line within which these goals are to be achieved", by supporting identity presentation and interaction with teachers, peers and external reviewers, and by recording academic development so as to promote metacognitive skills including monitoring and evaluation of progress. Learners can also share, collaborate and scaffold each other while learning.
requirements: An e-portfolio system that records learners' academic development and supports interaction with teachers, peers and external reviewers
target_learning_goals: Self-directed learning
Metacognitive monitoring and evaluation of progress
Collaborative meaning construction
examples: In the study, e-portfolio students wrote for each other and received feedback from peers and the teacher across a series of essays

article_title: E-Portfolio as a Corrective Platform towards EFL Students' Overall/Componential Writing Performance
citation: Saeedi, Z., & Meihami, H. (2015). E-Portfolio as a Corrective Platform towards EFL Students' Overall/Componential Writing Performance. Teaching English with Technology, 15(4), 76-97. http://www.tewtjournal.org
title: E-portfolio as a corrective feedback platform grounded in cognitive learning theory and self-regulation
description: The article frames EP-based corrective feedback within cognitive learning theory supporting deep learning processes of "creating, implementing, and evaluating L2". It explains the observed writing gains through self-regulation: feedback received via EP contributes to "feedback internalization" because students feel more responsible for their learning. EP's asynchronous, face-saving nature also lowers the affective filter, reducing anxiety compared with public corrective feedback.
requirements: Students must understand the corrective feedback platform to utilize the feedback received
constraints: Effectiveness depends on students' awareness of EP; without awareness, students may ignore implicit feedback
target_learning_goals: L2 writing improvement through internalized corrective feedback

article_title: Feasibility and implementation of a final year Objective Structured Clinical Examination (OSCE) in a medical model curriculum.
citation: Noll C, Mikuteit M, Golon S, Louzek C, Afshar K, Just I, Steffens S. (2026). Feasibility and implementation of a final year Objective Structured Clinical Examination (OSCE) in a medical model curriculum. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-10350-3
title: A structured, EPA-based station development process with interdisciplinary workshops and modified Angoff standard-setting.
description: The article describes a reproducible pattern for developing OSCE stations: an interdisciplinary team develops stations based on Entrustable Professional Activities, refines them in structured workshops involving students and standardised patient programme representatives, and sets pass–fail cut scores using the modified Angoff method. Stations were designed so that "at least 50.0% of the stations had to include a practical clinical skill", and each station included at least one communication subtask. This pattern enabled rapid design of 34 stations by subject-matter experts.
requirements: Requires an interdisciplinary project team with medical education, examination design, and specialist clinical knowledge.
Requires structured workshops with station developers, students, PJ-OSCE team members, and a standardised patient programme representative.
constraints: The article notes this was implemented within the specific curricular context of the HannibaL model curriculum at Hannover Medical School and the German medical licensing framework.
target_learners: Final-year undergraduate medical students prior to the Practical Year
target_learning_goals: Practical clinical skills
Clinical decision-making
Physician–patient communication
Interprofessional communication
examples: 34 PJ-OSCE stations were developed by 17 specialist physicians and five students, with 82.3% including clinical decision-making elements and 76.5% containing a skill.

Clinical competencies

article_title: Identifying clinical skill gaps of healthcare workers using a digital clinical decision support algorithm during outpatient pediatric consultations in primary health centers in Rwanda.
citation: Karoui Haykel, Rwandarwacu Victor P., Niyonzima Jonathan, Makuza Antoinette, Nkuranga John B., D'Acremont Valérie, Kulinkina Alexandra V. (2025). Identifying clinical skill gaps of healthcare workers using a digital clinical decision support algorithm during outpatient pediatric consultations in primary health centers in Rwanda. PLOS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0318284
title: ePOCT+ digital IMCI-based clinical decision support algorithm for outpatient pediatric care
description: ePOCT+ (electronic point of care tests plus) is a tablet-based digital clinical decision support algorithm implemented in 16 primary health centers in Rwanda as part of the DYNAMIC project. The article describes it as "a digital IMCI-based CDSA created to improve the quality of outpatient care for children under 15 years of age". Healthcare workers input anthropometric measures, vital signs, and symptom/sign presence following a logical consultation flow; the algorithm proposes diagnostic tests, then clinical diagnoses with management guidelines that can be accepted or rejected. All inputs are mandatory, with a limited 'not feasible' option, and it includes point-of-care devices such as pulse oximetry, hemoglobin and C-reactive protein measurement.
requirements: Accurate inputs (symptoms and signs) entered by healthcare workers, which relies on their clinical skills
Real-time use: perform the assessment, input the result, then move to the next proposed task
constraints: The article notes the dataset may be biased toward negative responses when healthcare workers answer without conducting the assessment
Alerts were unavailable to triage staff who wrote values on paper for later entry, and some inadequate measurements did not trigger alert thresholds
target_learners: healthcare workers in primary health centers in Rwanda
target_learning_goals: guiding outpatient pediatric consultations and proposing diagnoses and management plans
examples: Used for 20,085 consultations between November 2021 and October 2022 whose log data formed the retrospective analysis
key_sources: Karoui Haykel, Rwandarwacu Victor P., Niyonzima Jonathan, Makuza Antoinette, Nkuranga John B., D'Acremont Valérie, Kulinkina Alexandra V. (2025). Identifying clinical skill gaps of healthcare workers using a digital clinical decision support algorithm during outpatient pediatric consultations in primary health centers in Rwanda. PLOS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0318284

article_title: Evaluation of an e-learning platform promoting electronic personal health record competence: a pilot trial in older adults.
citation: Perotti Luis, Stamm Oskar, Ferizaj Drin, Dietrich Michael, Buchem Ilona, Müller-Werdan Ursula. (2025). Evaluation of an e-learning platform promoting electronic personal health record competence: a pilot trial in older adults. BMC Public Health. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12889-025-22242-0
title: ePA Coach: a microlearning-based e-learning platform with interactive ePHR mockups and a chat-based learning assistant for older adults
description: ePA Coach is a high-fidelity prototype learning platform developed as an "empowerment tool for self-sufficient ePHR usage". It offers 32 multimedia learning units (video and text, six to eight minutes each) across five competencies (basics, managing, adding, sharing and securing health data), organized into beginner, advanced and expert levels based on the EU DigComp framework, with gamification elements designed via the Octalysis framework. Interactive ePHR mockups let users practice navigation and tasks without real health data, and an always-available chat-based assistant built on RASA Conversational AI (107 intents, 1439 example questions, 217 responses) answers platform and ePHR questions; a moderated peer forum and glossary supplement the units.
requirements: Internet access and a device to access websites; participants needed basic digital skills to use the platform as a website
constraints: The article states that due to the design of the ePA Coach as a website, only those with access to the internet and basic digital skills could be included in the study
target_learners: Young-old adults aged 50–64 and older adults aged 65+ in Germany learning to use the electronic patient file (ePA)
target_learning_goals: ePHR knowledge, ePHR operation skills, and attitudes toward using the ePHR
examples: In the pilot trial, both age groups completed almost 80% of the 32 learning units during the one-week intervention period
key_sources: Perotti Luis, Stamm Oskar, Ferizaj Drin, Dietrich Michael, Buchem Ilona, Müller-Werdan Ursula. (2025). Evaluation of an e-learning platform promoting electronic personal health record competence: a pilot trial in older adults. BMC Public Health. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12889-025-22242-0

article_title: How Do Trainees Use EPAs to Regulate Their Learning in the Clinical Environment? A Grounded Theory Study.
citation: Thoonen Bart P. A., Scherpbier-de Haan Nynke D., Fluit Cornelia R. M. G., Stalmeijer Renée E. (2024). How Do Trainees Use EPAs to Regulate Their Learning in the Clinical Environment? A Grounded Theory Study. Perspectives on Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.5334/pme.1403
title: Three-stage model of trainees' EPA use across placements: adaptation, taking control, and checking the boxes
description: The article constructs a grounded theory in which trainees self-regulate learning by balancing helping and hindering influences of EPAs across three consecutive stages. As printed: "Three consecutive stages were constructed each with different use of EPAs: adaptation, taking control, and checking the boxes." Each stage appeared in both first and final year placements, with the adaptation phase typically shorter in the final year. The model was built from ten interviews plus two PICTOR interviews using constant comparative analysis.
requirements: Placements must be long enough for trainees to move from adaptation into the taking-control stage
constraints: Constructed from a single GP-training case at one Dutch medical centre; the authors note theoretical sufficiency may not have been fully achieved
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning in the clinical workplace
examples: Trainees in the adaptation phase deferred EPA use, while in the taking-control stage they scheduled specific patients and set learning objectives using EPAs

article_title: Skill retention following simulation learning in acute coronary syndrome versus cardiac arrest.
citation: Ghazali Hanen, Ouaness Islem, Zaouch Khedija, Hamed Rym, Ines Chermiti, Manai Hela. (2022). Skill retention following simulation learning in acute coronary syndrome versus cardiac arrest. La Tunisie Médicale. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9703463/
title: Episodic memory as the proposed mechanism for simulation-based learning and its retention
description: The article proposes episodic memory as one explanation of how simulator training produces learning and retention. It defines it as "la capacité d'un individu à se souvenir d'un événement vécu (sur simulateur) et de sa faculté à ressortir consciemment les informations mémorisées lorsqu'il revivra un événement identique (dans le réel)", i.e. recalling a lived simulated event and consciously retrieving the stored information when an identical event recurs in real practice. The article presents this as an advanced explanation rather than a mechanism tested in the study.
requirements: Exposure to a lived simulated event that can later be consciously recalled when an identical real event occurs
constraints: The article offers this as an explanatory concept cited from prior work, not as a mechanism tested in its own data
target_learners: young family-medicine residents in emergency departments
target_learning_goals: management of cardiac arrest and acute coronary syndrome emergencies
examples: The authors invoke episodic memory when discussing why simulator training may produce durable skills, citing prior work on difficult-airway mannequin training
key_sources: Ghazali Hanen, Ouaness Islem, Zaouch Khedija, Hamed Rym, Ines Chermiti, Manai Hela. (2022). Skill retention following simulation learning in acute coronary syndrome versus cardiac arrest. La Tunisie Médicale. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9703463/

article_title: Using an Entrustable Professional Activity to Assess Consultation Requests Called on an Internal Medicine Teaching Service.
citation: Kang Angela J., Gielissen Katherine, Windish Donna. (2019). Using an Entrustable Professional Activity to Assess Consultation Requests Called on an Internal Medicine Teaching Service. MedEdPORTAL. https://doi.org/10.15766/mep_2374-8265.10854
title: EPA-based consultation-request assessment instrument set (EPA document, Resident Supervisor Instrument, Intern Self-Reflection Instrument)
description: A set of three instruments built from an EPA delineating the knowledge, skills, and attitudes required to call a consultation request, developed from ACGME milestones, ten Cate et al.'s framework, Goldman's principles, and the PICO framework. The resident instrument assesses "the critical actions observable while the consultation request was being called," and the intern instrument supports self-reflection after feedback. Appendices A–E provide the EPA document, both instruments, an item-to-EPA correlation guide, and usage guidelines.
requirements: Participants received approximately 10 minutes of training on the use of the assessment instruments on the first or second day of their inpatient rotation
constraints: Not all critical actions from the EPA are assessed by items on the Resident Supervisor Instrument
The final critical action, "Intern follows up on consultation recommendations," was not observable during the call and was not evaluated
target_learning_goals: calling consultation requests
formulating PICO-centered clinical questions
calibrating required supervision level
examples: Used on two internal medicine inpatient teaching services at Yale New Haven Hospital from April through June of 2018, yielding 26 paired observations
key_sources: Kang Angela J., Gielissen Katherine, Windish Donna. (2019). Using an Entrustable Professional Activity to Assess Consultation Requests Called on an Internal Medicine Teaching Service. MedEdPORTAL. https://doi.org/10.15766/mep_2374-8265.10854

article_title: Predicting Bullying through Motivation and Teaching Styles in Physical Education.
citation: Montero-Carretero C., Barbado D., Cervelló E. (2020). Predicting Bullying through Motivation and Teaching Styles in Physical Education. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph17010087
title: Questionnaire battery measuring supportive style, need satisfaction, motivation, and bullying in PE
description: The study used four validated self-report instruments: the EPES-PE (19 items measuring organizational, procedural, and cognitive autonomy support plus controlling style, α = 0.94 for global AS), the Basic Psychological Needs in Exercise Scale adapted to PE (12 items, global α = 0.90), the CMPE motivation questionnaire (20 items across five motivation factors), and the Spanish European Bullying Intervention Project Questionnaire (EBIP-Q, 14 items, α = 0.83 for both perpetration and victimization).
requirements: Completed by students in approximately 20 minutes during a scheduled PE class with teacher clarification of doubts
constraints: Exclusive use of self-reports, noted by the authors as a main limitation
target_learning_goals: Assessment of teaching style, motivation, need satisfaction, and bullying behaviors in PE
key_sources: Montero-Carretero C., Barbado D., Cervelló E. (2020). Predicting Bullying through Motivation and Teaching Styles in Physical Education. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph17010087

article_title: Feasibility of the Epiduroscopy Simulator as a Training Tool: A Pilot Study.
citation: Lee Jong Joo, Ko Junho, Yun Yeomin, Jang Seong-Wook, Ha Yoon, Kim Yoon Sang, Shin Dong Ah. (2020). Feasibility of the Epiduroscopy Simulator as a Training Tool: A Pilot Study. Pain Research & Management. https://doi.org/10.1155/2020/5428170
title: EpiduroSIM: a virtual epiduroscopy simulator with joystick control and dual epiduroscopic/fluoroscopic views
description: EpiduroSIM is a virtual simulator built from a DICOM set of human CT data converted to 3D geometry and rendered in Unity 3D, controlled with a joystick. It "consists of three parts: visualization, training, and evaluation", models the spinal canal, intervertebral discs, dural sac, and spinal nerves, and displays both epiduroscopic and fluoroscopic views. It scores performance from an initial 100 points, deducting points for collisions and time, and records time to target, total score, and number of violations.
requirements: Requires additional equipment to operate, including a laptop and joystick controller
constraints: It is not available for commercial purchase
A haptic device was developed but not used because of a technical limitation in the actual experiments
target_learning_goals: catheter navigation to a target lesion site in the epidural space
anatomical understanding of the catheter insertion pathway
avoiding dura and nerve violation during epiduroscopy
examples: 20 physicians each performed the simulator 20 times in one day, navigating the catheter tip from the sacral hiatus to the posterior part of the L4-5 intervertebral disc without touching nerve or dura
